areas.about: Constraints tell Vivado what the clocks are, when signals arrive at the pins and which paths need no timing; timing closure is the work of making every remaining path fast enough. The agent writes the constraints from its skills, and a gate after routing fails any run that misses setup, hold or pulse-width timing or leaves a path unconstrained. A separate checker looks for risky lines, such as a false path with no stated reason.

After synthesis and after routing: no exception ignored or covering no path, no constraint message from an XDC line, no TIMING-24/-29/-47 or XDCH-1, and every multicycle path's registers share a real clock enable.
Before Vivado: a -setup N multicycle needs its -hold N-1, and a multicycle or datapath-only max delay needs a comment naming the enable or the synchroniser.

evidence.text: On 10 small designs with one timing-exception mistake each, Vivado itself said something about the exception in 5; the flow's checks flagged 10. They passed 4 of 4 correct designs.
On 13 small designs with one I/O-delay or virtual-clock mistake each, Vivado itself said something in 2; the flow's gates flagged 13.
On a two-clock probe design, setup slack on the crossing was -1.364 ns without AMD's macro exceptions and 8.891 ns with them (Vivado 2026.1).
Of the development runs whose saved designs were rebuilt on Vivado 2026.1, 6 reached routing; setup slack was positive in 6.

In 3 agent runs of the slow-controller drill (one clock, a one-in-eight enable, an eight-clock multicycle), the constraint grader passed 2; the other run put a register that a write sets on any clock into the eight-clock group, which only the grader's simulation check caught.

In 3 agent runs of the ADC-capture drill (input delays from a data sheet, the oscillator's jitter, a margin for implementation only), the delays were right in 3, free of made-up delays in 3 and carried the jitter in 3; the implementation-only margin was right in 0.

report_cdc must have no Critical row, after synthesis and after routing.

On the 12 mutants of the soak rig, its simulation with injection flagged 9.

rows.summary: MMCM VCO is 600-1200 MHz on a -1 7-series part but 800-1600 MHz on the K26; a ZU+ multiplier can be illegal on Artix-7.
7-series PLLE2 is a general clock generator; the UltraScale+ PLLE4 has no external feedback or deskew and is meant for I/O PHY clocking.
BUFR, BUFIO, BUFMR and BUFH exist only on 7-series; UltraScale+ uses BUFGCE, BUFGCE_DIV, BUFG_GT, BUFG_PS. Synthesis maps BUFG to BUFGCE and, measured, silently retargets BUFR and BUFIO.
A 7-series clock region spans half the device width; UltraScale+ regions are fixed-size tiles with segmented routing and distribution tracks, controlled with CLOCK_ROOT.
7-series has MRCC/SRCC clock-capable pins; UltraScale+ has GC pins on HP banks and HDGC pins on HD banks, and HDGC reaches only BUFGCE.
MMCME4 can change an output divider without a reset (CDDC); MMCME2 output changes need the DRP and a reset or relock.
Vivado retargets some 7-series clocking primitives on UltraScale+: an MMCME2_ADV in RTL synthesises to MMCME4_ADV, but the VCO limits then follow the new part.
CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE values differ: 7-series takes TRUE, BACKBONE or FALSE; UltraScale+ adds SAME_CMT_COLUMN and ANY_CMT_COLUMN, which 7-series does not have.

gaps: The Clocking Wizard's own settings were compared with the flow's search on only a few target frequencies.

The clock-mux check reads a netlist dump made in the check suite's Vivado session; it is not a stage gate, and the CE-select glitch it warns about was not shown in simulation (the unisim model has no timing).

rows.summary: Artix-7 and the Zynq-7020 have only HR banks (1.2-3.3 V); the K26 has HP banks (1.8 V maximum) and HD banks (up to 3.3 V).
IDELAYE2 has 32 taps of about 78 ps at a 200 MHz reference; IDELAYE3 has 512 taps of 2.1-12 ps and a TIME mode that holds a delay in picoseconds across voltage and temperature.
ISERDESE2/OSERDESE2 take widths up to 8 (14 cascaded) with BITSLIP; UltraScale+ ISERDESE3/OSERDESE3 take 4 or 8 with no bitslip, and native mode (RX/TX_BITSLICE) is a different design style.
On HR banks LVDS_25 outputs need VCCO 2.5 V and DIFF_TERM; on UltraScale+ HP banks LVDS runs at 1.8 V with DIFF_TERM_ADV, plus ODT and PRE_EMPHASIS that 7-series lacks.
Artix-7 has GTP transceivers (none on the Nexys A7 part) and the Zynq-7020 has none; the K26 has GTH transceivers with different wizards and reference-clock buffers.
7-series slices have CARRY4 and MUXF7/F8; UltraScale+ CLBs have one CARRY8 and MUXF9, and a 7-series CARRY4 instance has no ZU+ lib cell.

Artix-7 and the ZU+ PL have no hard Ethernet MAC: a fabric MAC drives a PHY through SelectIO (RMII, MII, RGMII). Both Zynq PS families have hard GEMs: RGMII through MIO, GMII through EMIO to PL logic.
RGMII's DDR registers are IDDR/ODDR on 7-series and IDDRE1/ODDRE1 on UltraScale+; both have a same-edge-pipelined input mode, but ODDRE1 has no opposite-edge mode.
Both families have 32-, 64-, 128- and 256-deep single-bit LUT RAMs; UltraScale+ adds RAM32M16, RAM64M8, RAM256X1D and RAM512X1S, so wide multi-port shapes and 512-deep columns exist only there.

rows.summary: UltraRAM (288 Kb, 4K x 72, one clock) exists on the K26 (64 blocks) but on no 7-series part; ram_style ultra has nothing to map to on Artix-7.
RAMB36E2 cascades data in the BRAM column (CASCADE_ORDER) with no fabric logic; RAMB36E1 only pairs two halves for a 64K x 1 memory.
Both families have 64-bit ECC in a RAMB36 in SDP mode; only RAMB36E2 adds an ECC pipeline register (EN_ECC_PIPE) for higher clock rates.
FIFO36E2 is not backward compatible with FIFO36E1: reset becomes synchronous, flag latencies change and asymmetric widths appear.
PL DRAM on Artix-7 uses MIG for DDR2/DDR3 on HR banks; the K26 uses the PS DDR4 controller, and a PL DDR4 controller (PG150) needs HP banks.
Both PS families have 256 KB OCM, but its address map and PL access path differ (Zynq-7000 through the GP/ACP ports, ZU+ through HPM/HPC/ACP and the LPD).

The memory controller's pin validation lives in the GUI and has no script command, so pins are checked against rules instead; that rule checker is not in this repository yet.

areas.about: A DMA engine moves blocks of data between memory and a stream, or between two memories, without the processor touching each word. The area covers the choice of engine (AMD's AXI DMA, central, multichannel and video DMA, the PCIe bridges, or a small engine written for the job), how descriptors, burst length and the number of bursts in flight set the throughput, the page-boundary rule every burst must keep, how a transfer's end is reported to software, and, on the Zynq processors, whether the caches see what the fabric reads and writes. The agent knows this from skills, asks the standing intake questions when a request moves blocks of data, and has an advisory check that flags a design reaching processor memory through a port that does not snoop the caches without a stated software contract. The library holds one engine of our own, simulated and proved against the AXI rules, and measured in simulation only: no board run exists yet.

checks.what: Advisory, from the spec's dma section and the port names in the sources: a design that reaches processor memory through a high-performance port, which does not snoop the caches, with no declared software cache contract; and a hardware-coherent contract declared on ports that are not coherent. Never fails a run.

Six standing questions added to the interview of a request that moves blocks of data: direction and buffer ownership, size and rate, the memory port, completion and interrupts, back pressure and errors, and the cache contract, each with a default and the reason for it.

evidence.text: In simulation against a memory with 20 clocks of read latency, our scatter-gather engine reads 0.2 of the memory port's limit for descriptors of 64 bytes, 0.94 for 4096 bytes and 0.98 for 16,384 bytes, with four bursts in flight; with one burst in flight it stays at 0.44. Descriptor overhead, not the data, sets the small-transfer figure.

20 of 22 seeded faults in the engine (a burst across a page boundary, a wrong length, a lost beat under back pressure, an ignored error response, a late interrupt and others) were caught by the simulation bench.

6 of 6 proofs by k-induction passed: the valid-held-until-ready rules on every channel the engine drives, burst size, alignment and the page-boundary rule, at three data widths in both directions; write data after its address and the burst limit are proved to a bounded depth only.

areas.about: Signal processing on an FPGA starts in software: the coefficients and word lengths of a filter or oscillator are designed first, then built into a datapath or an AMD core. The flow designs a filter in Python, measures what quantising it costs, generates the core and checks it word for word in AMD's simulator. These tools serve design work; none is a gate.

checks.what: Runs an AMD core in xsim from stimulus files, with a seeded valid and ready schedule, and compares every output word with a Python model. A tool for design work, not a stage gate.
Designs the FIR coefficients, quantises them, and reports the attenuation lost to the word length before the core is built.

evidence.text: The sine generator and oscillator-mixer tasks had 4 development runs; 3 passed every hidden test and 1 ended in an escape.
A decimating low-pass filter designed in Python came to 153 taps; rounding its coefficients to the core's word length cost 6.34018 dB of stop-band attenuation, and the specification was still met.
The generated filter core matched the integer model on all 1024 outputs in AMD's simulator: 0 mismatches with continuous input and 0 with random gaps.
Synthesised on its own, that core used 336 LUTs and 5 DSP slices, with 7.051 ns of setup slack at the target clock; that figure is before routing, so it is an upper bound.
The generated sine-generator core measured 96.2706 dB of spurious-free dynamic range against a target of 90 dB.

rows.summary: 7-series carry runs 4 bits per slice (CARRY4); UltraScale+ runs 8 bits per CLB (CARRY8), so adder delay per bit and the packing of short adders differ.
A single DSP takes 25 x 18 on 7-series and 27 x 18 on UltraScale+, which changes how wide multipliers and fixed-point formats split across slices.
The same RTL adder or multiplier closes at different clocks: -1 Artix-7 is the slowest of the owner's targets and the K26 -2LV runs at VCCINT 0.72 V.
Per-operator delays used to choose pipeline depth and hard resources before any build are measured per family; a 7-series model must not be reused on UltraScale+.

gaps: The int8 task escaped most often, and the misreading was of the spec, not of the arithmetic.

areas.about: A DSP slice is a multiplier and an adder with registers built into it. How fast a design that uses one can be clocked depends on which of those registers are turned on, and the agent writes them in the RTL so that synthesis packs them into the slice. Wider multiplies and long sums are built from several slices, either left to the tool or chained by hand, and each choice trades clocks of latency against clock speed and fabric logic. The agent knows this from skills and from measurements on two parts; an advisory check, not a gate, flags a slice with too few registers for the target clock period.

checks.what: Advisory, from the slices' register properties and the target clock period: flags a multiplier with no multiplier register, or a slice with no output register, at a period the measurements below say it cannot meet; a period below the slice's own minimum; and AMD's DPIP and DPOP rows. Never fails a run; a deliberately slow datapath may waive it with a reason.

evidence.text: Best clock speed against the number of registers around one multiply on the Artix-7 part, none to four registers: 175.2, 318.7, 326.6, 464.3 and 464.3 MHz. The step from two to three registers (the output register) is the large one; a fourth adds nothing (the register-count table in the results README; one routed run per point).

The same on the UltraScale+ part: 354.2, 571.4, 678, 725.2 and 725.2 MHz. The three-register figure is the clock-buffer limit of the part (the setup estimate at the target clock is higher); the data sheet's own DSP limit for the part is lower still and is the ceiling at sign-off.

On the Artix-7 part, a multiply of two narrow operands with operand, multiplier and output registers around it reached 464.3 MHz, which is the slice's own limit; with the output register left out it reached 326.6 MHz, and with no register at all 175.2 MHz (one routed run each, Vivado 2026.1).
On the UltraScale+ part the same three cases reached 725.2, 595.9 and 354.2 MHz; with every register the result is limited by the clock buffer (and the clock period asked for), not by the slice.

A single register after the multiply was packed into the slice's multiplier register (MREG 1, output register PREG 0) rather than its output register. With an asynchronous reset on that register it was packed into the output register instead, the multiplier stayed unregistered, and the slice ran at 198.9 MHz instead of 318.7 with a synchronous reset (Artix-7). AMD's methodology guide (UG949) describes this packing: the slice registers have synchronous resets only, so a register with an asynchronous reset is built in the fabric.

A signed multiply of two thirty-two-bit operands on the Artix-7 part, with the same registers at the ends: the tool's own split used 4 slices and reached 251.6 MHz; a hand-written cascade of slices (with the seventeen-bit shift) used 4 and reached 306.3 MHz; partial products summed in the fabric used 4 and reached 194.3 MHz.

An eight-term dot product on the Artix-7 part: a chain of slices (cascade) reached 464.3 MHz at 10 register stages; the same sum with a fabric adder tree, a register after every level, reached 328.4 MHz at 6 stages, so the tree saves clocks and loses speed.

The same two on the UltraScale+ part: the cascade reached 656.2 MHz at 10 stages (the delay registers that skew its operands became shift-register cells that limit the clock) and the tree 702.2 MHz at 6 stages.

A pre-adder before the multiplier was used by the slice and ran at 464.3 MHz with its own register and 290.4 MHz without it. A constant compare on an accumulator used the slice's pattern detector (PATDET); four twelve-bit adds written for the SIMD mode were not mapped to a slice (0 slices) with this coding.

figures.wrong: Latency here is register stages from the module's operand inputs to its product output; the two kept registers of the test wrapper are not counted. The speed is for one slice by itself: a real design adds routing from its own logic.

figures.caption: Slices used by a signed multiply wider than one slice, as the tool splits it, as a hand-written cascade, and with partial products summed in the fabric; for forty-eight by forty-eight the tool used 9 slices on Artix-7 against 6 for the cascade.

figures.wrong: The hand-written cascade was the fastest of the three at every width on both parts and used fewer slices than the tool's split for the two widest cases, but the tool's split used fewer or the same number of slices for the narrower ones. areas.about: RTL design is the core of the work: reading a spec, writing synthesisable code, pipelines and handshakes, hierarchy and register boundaries, and acting on lint and synthesis messages. One gate enforces the design standards on every run (no latches, no combinational loops, no gated clocks, synchronous resets), and another requires Vivado's methodology checks to show no critical warning.

checks.what: Design standards on the RTL: no latches, no combinational loops, no gated clocks, synchronous resets, declared crossings.

Advice after synthesis: a register whose non-zero initial value keeps it out of a DSP or block RAM, and an UltraRAM refused because of initial contents.

Check-suite gate (Brief 204a): a post-synthesis setup path that still fails with its net delay taken out cannot be closed by placement. Advisory RPT-LL-01 compares the logic-level distribution with the clock period.
Advisory (Brief 204a): a net with too many loads for its clock, with the guide's fixes (balanced tree with KEEP, a driver register, no MAX_FANOUT on global nets).
Check-suite gate (Brief 204a): control sets above the guide's required-reduction share of the device's capacity; the recommended-reduction band is an advisory.

evidence.text: In 2 Vivado 2026.1 syntheses of a multiply whose registers all start non-zero (two families), every one of those registers stayed out of the DSP block, with no warning; in 2 with them at zero, all went into it.

On Altera parts every core register starts at zero: in 6 Quartus Lite compiles (three families, NOT-gate push-back on and off) a RAM whose read register was to start non-zero was built from logic instead of a block RAM; in 3 with it at zero, a block RAM was used.
Across all 21 development runs, 13 passed every hidden test, 6 were escapes (the agent's own checks passed, the hidden tests did not) and 2 failed.

areas.about: Finite state machines carry the control in most designs. The skills cover separating control from counters, what a register on an input or an output costs in latency and timing, choosing an encoding and a reset (including a reset inside a clock-enable branch), running a slow machine on one fast clock, and checking that the tests reach every state and every legal transition. The coverage check is an evidence file that the flow can add to the second verification stage; it is off unless asked for.

checks.what: Synchronous-reset rule, no latch and no combinational loop; part of the standards stage gate that covers all RTL.
Reads the state register's value changes against the machine's state table: every state visited, every legal transition taken, none outside the table. Off unless the flag is given.
An input launched by another clock must pass two synchroniser registers; a direct use or a single register is flagged.

evidence.text: One controller built in Vivado two ways with the same behaviour: 11 states plus a counter (29 LUTs) and 23 states with the counter folded in (24 LUTs). Folding was the smaller; the split machine has 13 transitions to cover instead of 39.

At the test clock the slack from the state flops to an output pin was -1.859 ns with a decoded output and -0.437 ns with a registered one. A registered decode adds 1 clock of latency; registering the decode of the next state adds 0.

A state machine on a one-in-N clock enable, constrained with the multicycle pair on its own registers: slack between its registers was -0.659 ns without the exception and 1.283, 6.267 and 16.359 ns at three enable ratios.
The coverage check passed on 3 designs with their real tests, and failed, naming the missed state or transition, in 3 of 3 runs with one test removed.
A hand-built lift controller, a state machine with timers, passed its self-check on the board in 1 of 1 run.

areas.about: A signal that leaves the chip runs down a board trace, and the trace can send the edge back as overshoot and ringing at the receiver. The agent models one output at the pins: it takes the driver tables that AMD publishes for each I/O standard, the line's length and impedance and the receiver's capacitance, and finds out whether the receiver stays inside the data sheet's overshoot and undershoot limits, whether its first wave is large enough and whether the edge rings back through the threshold. It then proposes the drive strength, slew rate and series resistor. A finished board cannot always change its resistor, so it gives two answers for each port: the best setting for the board as built, and the best setup if the resistor can change. The check is advisory, nothing in the flow stops a run that disagrees with it, and every figure here is a model result, not a scope measurement.

checks.what: Advisory check of every output port group of a design against the receiver limits in the data sheet (overshoot and undershoot with their duration tables, first-wave level, ringback), reading the part family from the spec. It gives two answers per group: the best DRIVE and SLEW with the board's own series resistor, and the best series resistor with its DRIVE and SLEW; a group marked board_fixed gets the first.
The solver under the check: a transmission line between AMD's IBIS output models and a capacitive receiver, at the three IBIS corners, with the first-incident level and the ringback.

evidence.text: A sweep of 868 model runs (DRIVE, SLEW, series resistor and line length, three IBIS corners in each) found that 22 ohm in series on a 6 in line passes 0 of 8 DRIVE and SLEW combinations for LVCMOS33 in 7-series HR banks, against 6 of 8 with 47 ohm, and 8 of 15 for LVCMOS18 in UltraScale+ HP banks.

With the KR260 carrier's measured routing (port A 7.2 in, port B 2.8 in, no series resistor on either), the transmit pins as the design sets them (DRIVE 12 mA FAST) put the receiver 1.06 V beyond the rail on port A and 1 V on port B, against the 0.2 V limit; the model puts that right with 27 ohm in series on port A and 22 ohm on port B.

With no resistor on the board, no setting meets every limit on port A: the best, DRIVE 4 mA, keeps the overshoot inside the limit but its receiver edge takes 2.08 ns at the weak corner against the 1 ns the house rule allows. If a resistor can be fitted, 7 combinations pass, and the check proposes 27 ohm.
A second solver, ngspice, run on 24 cases with a series resistor, agreed with the model's receiver waveform to within 0.04 V.
On 12 falling edges with nothing in series the two solvers disagree by up to 0.59 V; the cause is not found.
Routed lengths read from the vendor's KR260 board file: the 15 length-matched RGMII nets of port A run 7.07 to 7.34 in on the carrier.
The 14 length-matched RGMII nets of port B run 2.34 to 2.87 in.

gaps: No board scope measurement: every waveform and number is a model result on AMD's preliminary IBIS data, so none of it has been compared with a real edge.
The dielectric constant of the carrier is not in its board file, so the line impedance is the fabricator's table value, and two solvers disagree about it by about a sixth.
The routing inside the K26 module is missing, so every length is carrier copper only and the real lines are longer.
ngspice and the model disagree on falling edges with nothing in series and the cause is not found, so the falling-edge rows without a resistor may understate the ringing.
The survey of series resistor values counted one board only, so the belief that 22 ohm is the commonest value is neither confirmed nor refuted.
Calibrated drivers (DCI, OUTPUT_IMPEDANCE) are not simulated in the time domain, and simultaneous-switching noise is left to Vivado's own report, which has not been run for these designs.
The knowledge bank at its pin has the I/O standard skills and a family-matrix row for drive, slew and output resistance, but no skill on choosing a series resistor.
The check is advisory and is not a gate in any stage, no agent run has been scored on it, and no result in this area comes from Vivado or a board, so the level stays at knowledge only.
